title: Buildings the City rents: when the landlord’s building last changed hands
question: Was a building bought shortly before the City signed a lease in it, did it change hands while the City was the tenant, and how does a year’s rent compare with the building’s assessed value?
finding: 122 of the 126 Board files with the City as tenant could be matched to a parcel, at 78 sites; the rolls give a sale date before the lease for 72. 7 new leases were introduced within two years after the building’s last sale date (945 Bryant Street, 162 days; 888 Post Street, 195 days; 1360 Mission Street, 256 days; 250 Kearny Street, 371 days; 258A Laguna Honda Boulevard, 475 days; 2000 Oakdale Avenue, 508 days; 752 Vallejo Street, 628 days); 2 buildings changed hands again within two years after a new City lease (945 Bryant Street, sale dated 1 May 2019, value set $42,791,550 against $27,540,000 on the roll before; 1076 Howard Street, sale dated 18 July 2022, value set $17,886,207 against $10,394,832 on the roll before); at 2 sites a sale date falls between the first and last lease file on record. Where a sale within three years set a value and the title states the rent (2 leases), a year’s rent is 6% to 10% of that value for the space the City took.
how: Every passed Board file with the City as tenant, matched to parcels by address. The prior sale is the latest sale date on any roll from 2007 to 2025 before the file was introduced. Files at the same parcels are read as one tenancy, from the first file on record to the last. Rent is the first-year rent the property screens read from the file title. Assessed value is land plus improvements on the last roll before the file (or the value a just-completed sale set, where the roll had not caught up), scaled to the City’s share of the building where the title gives square feet and the roll gives the building’s floor area. Rent against the value a sale set is shown only when that sale was within three years. A later sale is listed when its date falls within two years after a new lease was introduced, with the assessed value on the roll before it and the value it set.
limits: A landlord buying a building with a tenant in view, or with the City already in it, is ordinary commercial practice, and a long lease to a government tenant makes a building worth more to the next buyer, the more so where the lease came with building work; City leases are negotiated, and above a set rent the law requires an appraisal that is not in these files. Board files start in 2014, so a first file on record may be the renewal of a much older lease. A high rent against assessed value mostly marks a building held for decades, whose assessed value is far below its market value; it is a question only where the value was set by a recent sale. Floor areas on the roll are often missing or cover several buildings. The roll records no price. The value that appears after a sale date is an indicator of the price, because California law re-sets assessed value to the price paid when a property changes hands; exemptions, a transfer of part of a property, transfers the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break that link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder would settle what was paid; neither is open data. The roll names no owners: that the landlord in the file bought on the prior sale date is an inference.
